title: Quadrilaterals Grade 3: Squares, Rectangles & More (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Quadrilaterals Grade 3: Shapes Made Simple + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach quadrilaterals in Grade 3 the easy way: count sides and corners, tell a square from a rhombus, sort shapes, and try a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: A quadrilateral is just any closed shape with four straight sides. Here is how I help Grade 3 children see the family — square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium — and tell them apart, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 3 child a chocolate bar, a window frame, a kite and a slice of samosa, and ask what they have in common. After a bit of squinting, someone will say ‘they all have four sides.’ That is the whole idea behind quadrilaterals grade 3 sets out to teach: a quadrilateral is any closed shape made from four straight sides. Nothing more mysterious than that. The word looks scary — ‘quad’ means four, ‘lateral’ means side — but the shapes are ones your child already sees a hundred times a day.

The tricky part is not spotting four sides. It is learning that a square, a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram and a trapezium are all cousins in one family, each with its own small rule. In my experience teaching eight-year-olds, the shapes click far faster when you stop drawing them on a board and start counting sides and corners on real objects at home.

What makes a shape a quadrilateral?

Two things, both easy to check. First, the shape must be closed — no gaps, so you could trace the whole outline and end up where you started. Second, it must have exactly four straight sides. That also means four corners (we call them vertices).

  • A triangle has three sides, so it is not a quadrilateral.
  • A circle has no straight sides, so it is out too.
  • A shape with a gap in its outline is not closed, so it does not count.
  • Anything with four straight sides that joins up — even a wonky one — is a quadrilateral.

I like to give children a ‘four-and-closed’ test. Count the straight sides; if you get four, and the outline is fully joined, it belongs to the family. That single test sorts most shapes correctly before we ever name them.

Meet the common quadrilaterals

Once a child is happy that a shape has four sides, the next step is telling the cousins apart. They differ in two ways only: the length of their sides and whether their corners are right angles (the neat square corner you can check with the edge of a book).

Square

Four equal sides and four right angles. A carrom board, a chessboard, a paper napkin folded once. It is the tidiest quadrilateral — everything about it matches.

Rectangle

Opposite sides equal and four right angles, but the sides are not all the same length — it is longer one way. A door, a mobile phone, a currency note of ₹100. Children often call a rectangle a ‘long square,’ which is a surprisingly good instinct.

Rhombus

Four equal sides like a square, but the corners are pushed over, so they are not right angles. The classic example is a diamond on a playing card, or many kites flown at Sankranti. Same side lengths as a square, tilted corners.

Parallelogram

Opposite sides equal and parallel, corners pushed over. Think of a rectangle that has been nudged sideways, like a leaning name-plate. The eraser-shaped shapes in a maths kit are a good example.

Trapezium

The odd one out: only one pair of sides is parallel. A handbag flap, or the side view of a bucket that is wider at the top. It still has four sides, so it is firmly in the family.

A shape-by-shape comparison

QuadrilateralSidesRight anglesEveryday object
Square4 equal4Carrom board
RectangleOpposite sides equal4Door
Rhombus4 equal0Playing-card diamond
ParallelogramOpposite sides equal0Leaning name-plate
TrapeziumOne pair parallel0 or moreBucket side view

Here is the one counter-intuitive point worth planting early: a square is also a special rectangle, and also a special rhombus. It follows both rules at once. Do not force this on a Grade 3 child in the first week, but if a bright student asks whether a square counts as a rectangle, the honest answer is yes — and they will feel clever for spotting it.

Counting sides, corners and right angles

Naming shapes matters less than counting them accurately. Give your child three columns on a page — sides, corners, right angles — and a pile of cut-out shapes to fill it in. The counting itself does the teaching.

  • Trace each side with a finger and say the number out loud — it stops double-counting.
  • Check right angles with the corner of a book or a folded paper; if the corner fits snugly, it is a right angle.
  • Mark each corner with a small dot so none is missed.

A quick caveat from the classroom: children love to guess the name before counting. Slow them down. The counting is the skill the exam actually tests; the name is just the label that follows.

Sorting quadrilaterals from the rest

Once counting is solid, play a sorting game. Draw a big circle on paper labelled ‘quadrilaterals’ and drop shapes inside or outside it. Triangles, circles and open zig-zags stay out; squares, rectangles, kites and trapeziums go in. This ‘is it or isn’t it’ sorting is exactly how school worksheets frame the topic, and it builds the habit of applying the four-and-closed test every time.

Spotting quadrilaterals around the house

End the week with a shape hunt. Ask your child to find and name ten four-sided objects — a television, a book cover, a floor tile, a road sign, a chapati board. This is where the topic stops being a worksheet and becomes something they notice everywhere, which is the whole point.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight-question quiz below checks exactly these ideas — counting sides and corners, telling the cousins apart, and sorting shapes as quadrilateral or not. Let your child answer, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they want more written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Quadrilaterals Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on four-sided shapes: counting sides and corners, naming quadrilaterals, and sorting them from other shapes. Pick an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How many sides does a quadrilateral have?
questions.explanation: ‘Quad’ means four, so every quadrilateral has exactly four straight sides.

questions.q: Which shape is NOT a quadrilateral?
questions.explanation: A triangle has only three sides, so it cannot be a quadrilateral.

questions.q: A shape has four equal sides and four right angles. What is it?
questions.explanation: Four equal sides plus four right angles makes a square.

questions.q: How many corners (vertices) does a rectangle have?
questions.explanation: A rectangle has four sides, so it also has four corners.

questions.q: Which quadrilateral has only ONE pair of parallel sides?
questions.explanation: A trapezium is the one with just a single pair of parallel sides.

questions.q: A rhombus is most like a square because it has four equal sides. How is it different?
options: Its corners are not right angles
questions.explanation: A rhombus has four equal sides like a square, but its corners are pushed over, so they are not right angles.

questions.q: Which everyday object is shaped like a rectangle?
questions.explanation: A door has opposite sides equal and four right angles, so it is a rectangle.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a quadrilateral?
questions.explanation: A circle has no straight sides at all, so it is not a quadrilateral.

faq.q: What is a quadrilateral in simple words for Grade 3?
faq.a: It is any closed shape with four straight sides — and so four corners. Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, parallelograms and trapeziums are all quadrilaterals.

faq.q: How is a square different from a rhombus?
faq.a: Both have four equal sides. A square has four right-angle corners; a rhombus has its corners pushed over, so they are not right angles. Think of a rhombus as a tilted square.

faq.q: Is a square also a rectangle?
faq.a: Yes. A square follows the rectangle rule — four right angles — and adds that all four sides are equal, so it is a special rectangle. Grade 3 children do not need to worry about this, but it is correct.

faq.q: How do I help my child tell the shapes apart?
faq.a: Focus on two checks only: are the sides equal, and are the corners right angles? Use the edge of a book to test a right angle. Counting sides and corners on real objects at home works far better than memorising names.
